components.summary: A fixed 5 V, 3 A buck regulator needing only four external parts — the classic drop-in replacement for a 7805.
The archetypal optocoupler in surface mount — and the "-C" on the end of the order code narrows its gain far more than the catalog suggests.
An RGB LED with its own controller inside — chain hundreds of them and drive the whole string from one pin.
A 70 V, −55 °C optocoupler whose "-B-" order code names a gain rank the catalog's 50–600 % span ignores.
Standalone linear lithium charger in SOT-23-6 — 4.2 V within ±1 %, up to 500 mA set by a single resistor.
Puts a 3.3 V microcontroller's CAN controller onto a real CAN bus, with slope control and a standby mode.
A MAX232 that works from 3.3 V as well as 5 V, with ±15 kV ESD protection and smaller capacitors.
A 16 MHz crystal with a 9 pF load — the classic Arduino Uno clock frequency.

The Arduino Uno's microcontroller — 8-bit AVR, 32 kB flash, and the widest supply range of any MCU here.
The P-channel companion to the AO3400A — for high-side switching and reverse-polarity protection.

components.summary: The 5 V member of the same CMOS LDO family — 25 mV dropout at light load, 2.5 µA quiescent, from up to 30 V in.
Charges a single lithium cell from USB with one resistor setting the current — and no protection whatsoever.

components.manufacturer: Jing Extension of the Electronic Co.
components.summary: A 16-contact USB Type-C receptacle, USB 2.0 only, rated 3 A — but the drawing on file carries a different part number.
The industrial-temperature LM358 — same silicon, −40 °C to +105 °C, for a fraction of a cent more.
Dual-core 133 MHz Cortex-M0+ with 264 kB RAM and no internal flash — you add your own QSPI flash chip.
The default small N-channel switch — turns on properly from 2.5 V logic, and there are 1.6 million in stock.
An eight-way analog switch — three address pins pick which of eight signals connects to the common pin.
A plain red 0603 indicator LED — the cheapest way to tell a user something is happening.
A white 0603 indicator LED specified at 5 mA — and with up to 3.1 V of forward drop, an awkward fit on a 3.3 V rail.
ST's value-line 48 MHz Cortex-M0 in the same LQFP-48 outline as the F103, at roughly two-thirds the price.
The six-axis motion sensor behind a decade of hobby projects — with an exposed pad the datasheet tells you not to solder.
Four diodes wired as a bridge in one small package — turns AC into DC, or makes a supply polarity-proof.
Makes real RS-232 voltages from a single 5 V rail — the chip that killed the ±12 V supply.
A board-edge 16-contact USB Type-C receptacle rated 3 A at 5 V, with over a million in stock — and not a six-pin power-only part.
A small logic-level N-channel MOSFET — the one inside every bidirectional I²C level shifter.

components.manufacturer: Jiangsu Changjing Electronics Technology Co., Ltd.
components.summary: A programmable shunt reference — the TL431 in a SOT-23, for setting a voltage precisely from two resistors.
One chip that can be wired as a step-down, step-up, or voltage-inverting converter — unusually flexible, and old.
The 32.768 kHz watch crystal a real-time clock needs — and its accuracy falls off as the square of how far you are from room temperature.
Standalone linear lithium charger in SOT-23-5 — 4.2 V within ±1 %, charge current set by a single resistor.
Ethernet on an SPI bus — TCP/IP runs inside the chip, so your microcontroller does not need a network stack.
The LM2596's older, slower sibling — same 5 V at 3 A, but 52 kHz switching means much larger magnetics.
Two small Schottky diodes sharing a cathode — for clamping, OR-ing two supplies, or protecting an input.
A 1 A, 1000 V ultrafast rectifier — high voltage and quick to turn off, where a Schottky cannot reach.
A tighter-tolerance optocoupler — its datasheet puts the "B" grade's current transfer ratio in a 2:1 band, 130–260 %.
A high-gain optocoupler in SOP-4 whose order code names its 200–400 % gain grade — and the grade letter is printed on the part.
512 Mbit (64 MB) of 1.8 V SPI NAND in an eight-pin package, with single-bit error correction built into the chip.
The cheapest microcontroller in the catalog — 16 MHz 8-bit, 5 V tolerant supply, 8 kB flash, in hand-solderable TSSOP-20.
A current-generation 64 MHz Cortex-M0+ in a hand-solderable 20-pin package, with 32 kB flash and 8 kB RAM.

components.summary: A 3.3 V, 200 mA LDO drawing about a microamp idle — and a dropout whose guaranteed maximum is nearly three times the headline figure.

Four two-input AND gates — output high only when both inputs are high.
Six Schmitt-trigger inverters — the standard cure for a noisy, slow, or bouncing digital signal.
The input counterpart of the 74HC595 — reads eight switches or signals back through three pins.
Eight bidirectional buffers with a direction pin — the standard way to isolate or strengthen a parallel bus.

components.summary: A 5 V, 500 mA three-terminal regulator — the classic 7805 in a surface-mount package, with ±2 % accuracy.
Turns three microcontroller pins into eight outputs, and chains so you can have as many as you like.
A fixed 5 V, 2 A buck converter from up to 40 V — with an enable pin that is active low, not high.

components.category: Voltage Regulators - Linear, Low Drop Out (LDO) Regulators
components.summary: The 3.3 V rail on countless dev boards — 1 A, cheap, and with over a million in stock here.

32 kilobytes of I²C EEPROM, addressable eight to a bus, running from anything between 1.7 V and 5.5 V.
Two four-way analog switches that share their address pins — the differential sibling of the CD4051B.
Turns a USB port into a serial port with no crystal and no external resistors — just the chip and a connector.
512 Mbit (64 MB) of 1.8 V NOR flash in an AEC-Q100 automotive grade rated to 125 °C — a code store for hot places, at a price to match.
A 5 V RS-485 transceiver with ±15 kV ESD protection built in — for buses that leave the enclosure.
A 5 V CAN transceiver designed for low emissions, with input levels that accept 3.3 V logic.
A dual JFET-input op-amp — fast, quiet, and with essentially no input current, which is why guitar pedals use it.
The original 5 V RS-485 transceiver — one driver, one receiver, and a bus that tolerates −7 V to +12 V.
Four op-amps in one package, running from a single supply with inputs that work down to ground.

components.summary: The small 5 V regulator — 100 mA, three terminals, and a design that has not changed since the 1970s.
Managed flash storage in one chip — an 8 GB part with 7.28 GB usable, effectively a soldered-down disk for an embedded Linux board.
The blue 0603 indicator in the curated picks — and its absolute maximum forward current is only 10 mA.
The green 0603 indicator in the curated picks — an InGaN part that leaves a 3.3 V rail almost no resistor headroom.
Two rail-to-rail op-amps that run from 1.8 V and draw 100 µA — the modern replacement for an LM358.
The adjustable XL1509 — 1.23 V to 37 V at 2 A, with the same active-low enable pin as the fixed versions.
A 1 A, 40 V Schottky rectifier — the standard catch diode for small buck converters, and its leakage climbs a hundredfold when hot.
A tiny bidirectional 5 V ESD clamp for slower signal lines — too much capacitance for USB data.
The audio designer's default dual op-amp — 5 nV/√Hz of noise and enough output current to drive headphones.
A precision op-amp with 60 µV of offset and no need for trim components — accurate, but slow.
A low-power I²C real-time clock with alarm, timer and a programmable clock output — 0.25 µA on backup.
One buffer in a five-pin package — the standard trick for driving a WS2812 strip from 3.3 V logic.
Two fast silicon switching diodes in series in a tiny package — for clamping, steering and protection.
Seven low-side switches in one chip, each good for 500 mA at up to 50 V, with built-in flyback diodes.
Drives a segment LCD so your microcontroller does not have to — 128 segments over three wires, plus a buzzer output.

Two comparators with open-collector outputs — for turning an analog threshold into a clean digital signal.
A single low-voltage op-amp in a tiny 5-pin package — runs from 2.7 V, swings to the rails, sips 130 µA.
8 kilobytes of I²C non-volatile storage — thirty-two times the M24C02, for a couple of cents more.
The bigger STM8 — 32 kB flash, 2 kB RAM and a full 1 kB of EEPROM, still running from 5 V.
The cheap USB-to-serial bridge — the alternative to a CP2102 when cost matters more than driver support.
Protects four fast data lines from static discharge without slowing them down — 3.5 pF, in a six-pin package.
The "Blue Pill" chip — 72 MHz Cortex-M3 with USB and CAN, 64 kB flash and 20 kB RAM in LQFP-48.
Keeps the date and time running on a backup cell, and can trickle-charge that cell for you.
RS-485 from a single 3.3 V rail, pin-compatible with the classic 75176 — the modern default for new designs.
A 12 MHz crystal with a 20 pF load — the frequency the RP2040's USB bootloader requires.

Two logic signals across a 2.5 kV galvanic barrier — one in each direction, in an ordinary 8-pin SOIC.

The battery-life specialist — 0.3 µA in standby, 4 kB of real EEPROM, and USB, in the familiar LQFP-48 outline.
A 3 A buck converter that takes anything from 5.5 V to 36 V and needs almost no external parts.
A 3 A buck converter that starts from 3.5 V, skips pulses at light load, and costs about 44 cents.

families.summary: Current-controlled switches and amplifiers — still the cheapest way to drive a small load from a logic pin.
Four diodes in one package that turn AC into DC — at the cost of two diode drops.
The most numerous parts in the catalog — thick-film chip resistors from 0402 to 1206, all from one manufacturer.
Quartz resonators — the reason your USB enumerates and your clock does not drift.
The cheapest user interface there is — and the one thing on a board people notice first.
Bulk capacitance where ceramics run out — and the two failure modes you need to respect.
Two parts that look identical and do opposite jobs — one stores energy, the other deliberately wastes it.
Voltage-controlled switches — nearly no drive current, and milliohms instead of a diode drop.
The decoupling capacitor you place hundreds of — and the one whose real capacitance is often half what the label says.
Four resistors of the same value in one body — for pull-ups and series termination on a bus.

The push button — a mechanical part on an electronic board, with mechanical specifications to match.

Diodes designed to conduct backwards at a known voltage — for clamping, simple regulation and protection.
